title: Learning to Macromanage
description: The people as a team do the thing, whether it’s running a company or winning a national championship, and you lead them to do it well, like Pat did. Their achievement is your achievement, the team’s achievement, so you train them to do it well. Then get out of the way.

blocks.alt: Rise course cover image shown on the course start screen

blocks.markdown: OK, so, you’re responsible for your area. The buck stops with you. You have accountability. You have ownership. Now, how do you take responsibility for all the moving parts without micromanaging the details? If you’re going to be responsible for everything, you have to make sure everything is running smoothly. If you’re going to be responsible for making sure everything is running smoothly, you need to be involved in the details, right? I mean, how can you ensure a successful outcome if you don’t know everything that’s going on? Not so fast…

The truth is, some leaders — well-meaning leaders — get this far into understanding responsibility and ownership and then get stuck. Their extreme sense of responsibility spills over into the dreaded world of micromanaging. Click on each circle in the illustration below for examples of micromanaging.

sections.title: Making every decision
sections.body: Sitting in on every new hire interview

blocks.markdown: Maybe this rings a bell with you or someone you know. After all, that’s unconditional ownership, right? Not necessarily.

sections.title: If you have a company of 10 people total, maybe some of these responsibilities d
sections.body: If you have a company of 10 people total, maybe some of these responsibilities do fall on you. Chances are, though, you’re not in that category. Or maybe you started in that category and grew out of it long ago, but you’re still operating like you’re a one-person band.

sections.title: And know what’s worse?
sections.body: And know what’s worse? It starts to crush those you lead. With your fingers in every pie, the team never learns how to cook, metaphorically speaking. People either gravitate toward two areas: They don’t think for themselves (why would they, if you’re going to wind up making every decision for the group?) or they’re so terrified to make a mistake they can’t do anything without approval. They default to order-takers, and any unique characteristics or skills you hired them for in the first place get buried.

sections.title: If your time had a dollar amount of what you’re worth to the company (not your l
sections.body: If your time had a dollar amount of what you’re worth to the company (not your literal hourly wage, but the amount of money your decisions bring in per month), would the best use of your time be researching costs for a new type of coffee in the break room or rewriting the second paragraph of the company newsletter? What about sitting in four meetings each week about processes and procedures? Deciding whether a button on a website will be green or blue? What picture should go in the new brochure?Probably none of the above. There are certain things that only you can do, and it’s most important to make time for those.

sections.title: Exercise
sections.body:
Which of these is an unintended outcome of micromanaging?
Drag and drop each card to complete this element.

blocks.prompt: You'll see one item at a time. Decide whether it belongs with “Outcome of Micromanaging” or “Outcome of Macromanaging”.

cards.text: It takes your time away from other more important duties.
Your team learns to do things on their own.
It starts to crush those you lead.
It’s unscalable.
Your team won’t learn to think for themselves.
Your team will be terrified to make mistakes.
The team becomes order-takers.
The team will be hesitant to do anything without approval.
Your teammates learn when to consult you and when to take risks.
Team members like it.
You will have more free time in your day.

blocks.markdown:
When leaders realize that wearing themselves out over details like the above is not only making them tired, but squashing their team, it can be a freeing revelation. So, how do you hold yourself responsible for all the things that can go right or wrong without being involved in the day-to-day operations? Part of it goes back to the classic definition of leadership. You may have heard it before:
You manage things, and you lead people.

The people as a team do the thing, whether it’s running a company or winning a national championship, and you lead them to do it well, like Pat did. Their achievement is your achievement, the team’s achievement, so you train them to do it well. Then get out of the way.

That’s it. That doesn’t mean you don’t step in in an emergency. That doesn’t mean you’re always in the dark. You don’t do it for them, you don’t do it with them. You hire smart people, people who are a good fit, and make sure they have what they need to do their job well.

What Does It Take to Be "Hands-Off"?

Understanding the importance of being “hands off” is one of the most fundamental (and often overlooked) tenets of good leadership.

Sometimes as a leader, we think our strength lies in getting the team to produce a certain level of output — after all, it’s what we’re all responsible for. You may even be tempted to jump in and help them. But at the end of the day, you can’t make people do things. You have to lead them. All you can really do is hire well.

We’ll say it again. All you can really do is get the right people in the right seat on the bus and lead them well to do their jobs. You can’t force them to do it with excellence, innovation, positivity, super-service, or creativity. All you can do is fire them if they don’t and replace them with someone else who will. Then the cycle starts again.

As the leader, you have to lead them in attitude, vision, excellence, motivation — all the principles Pat championed in the Definite Dozen — guiding them to the level of self-discipline, autonomy, or ingenuity you want. They will know what that level is because it will be modeled by you. Not done by you on behalf of the team or for the team but encouraged by the level of leadership you provide.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of micromanaging?

choices.text: Setting clear goals for the team
Asking your admin to automatically include you on every department meeting
Letting your team present new ideas

questions.prompt: What are some of the disadvantages of micromanaging as a leader?

choices.text: Your team won’t learn to think for themselves.
